accessibility.text: One reason for taking parallelism seriously is that causal connections between the physical and mental realms can look very puzzling.
A third answer is: No. Physical and phenomenal properties cannot causally interact.
A second argument is also simple. Once we think that there are no causal connections between the physical and mental worlds at all, why should we keep believing in a physical world at all?
Each of these views has its own strengths and weaknesses.
interactionism
This thought puts some pressure on the parallelist to become an idealist, who denies that there is any physical world at all.
Ann tastes the apple and feels less hungry.
Ann feels hunger, and decides to walk to the fridge.
parallelism
Here is what our causal chain looks like, according to the idealist.
Ann has a visual sensation of an apple and decides to eat it.
epi-phenomenalism
Let’s start with the parallelist. This looks like the craziest of the three views -- why would anyone hold it?
One answer is: Yes. Physical properties can cause phenomenal properties, and phenomenal properties can cause physical properties.
A second answer is: Yes. Physical properties can cause phenomenal properties; but phenomenal properties cannot cause physical properties.

There are no fridges, or doors, or apples, or walking -- just experiences as if there were such things. The fact that parallelism seems to lead to this sort of idealist view seems to many to be a reason to reject it.
